# Exact single-fiber enlargement reserve and its facet cap response
hypotheses. It does not assert that an attained bad minimum has an
available reserve facet or a favorable cap response.

The facet first-variation formulas have antecedents in
selective-localization-first-variation.md. Arbitrary small independent
fiber changes under *global strict compatibility* were proved in
two-sided-local-mass-variations-and-compatible-hull-bump-obstruction.md.
The additional ingredient here is an exact finite description of the
largest allowable *single-fiber enlargement region*, incorporating every
anchored constraint. It can be used when many other compatibility
constraints are tight. The companion centroid-defect examples show that
positive midpoint volume or centroid deficits alone do not supply this
reserve.

## 1. Setting and all anchored constraints

Let \(P=\operatorname{conv}(P)\cap\mathbb Z^n\) be finite and nonempty,
with full affine span in the integer base space. Let \(d\ge1\) and
let \(K_p\subset\mathbb R^d\) be positive-volume compact polytopes.
Assume that their hull over \(P\) has exactly these integer fibers.
Equivalently, every anchored convex combination satisfies
\[
 \sum_r\lambda_rK_r\subset K_q
 \quad\text{whenever}\quad
 \lambda_r\ge0,\quad\sum_r\lambda_r=1,\quad
 \sum_r\lambda_rr=q\in P.                               \tag{1}
\]
Write \(h_p(u)=\max_{x\in K_p}u\cdot x\).

For each \(q\in P\) let
\[
 {\cal A}_q=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R^{P\setminus\{q\}}:
       \lambda_r\ge0,\ \sum_{r\ne q}\lambda_r=1,\
       \sum_{r\ne q}\lambda_rr=q\}.
\]
This polytope may be empty. Let \({\cal V}_q\) be its finite set of
extreme points, empty when \({\cal A}_q\) is empty. Fix an irredundant
facet description of each \(K_q\), with outward unit normals
\({\cal N}_q\).

Fix a fiber \(p\). Define the closed convex polyhedron
\[
 {\cal R}_p=
 \bigcap_{\substack{q\ne p,\ \lambda\in{\cal V}_q\\
                         \lambda_p>0,\ u\in{\cal N}_q}}
 \left\{x:\ u\cdot x\le
  \frac{h_q(u)-\sum_{r\ne p,q}\lambda_rh_r(u)}
       {\lambda_p}\right\}.                            \tag{2}
\]
An empty intersection of constraints means all of \(\mathbb R^d\).
This definition uses actual supporting planes of target fibers,
not volume-root inequalities.

## 2. Exact enlargement theorem

**Theorem 1.** The original \(K_p\) is contained in \({\cal R}_p\).
For any compact convex \(L\supset K_p\), replace only \(K_p\) by \(L\)
and keep every other fiber fixed. This replacement is an actual family
on the same complete base if and only if
\[
                         L\subset{\cal R}_p.           \tag{3}
\]

**Proof.** The original support inequalities (1), tested at each
target facet normal, give the containment of \(K_p\) in (2).
Necessity of (3) follows by applying (1) to each displayed extreme
representation and each displayed target facet.

Conversely assume (3). At a target \(q\ne p\), an extreme anchored
representation with \(\lambda_p>0\) satisfies every facet inequality
of \(K_q\) by (2). One with \(\lambda_p=0\) is unchanged. Thus
every extreme representation is feasible. Any other representation
in \({\cal A}_q\) is a convex combination of these extremes, and
the support-function inequalities remain valid after taking that
combination. A representation which uses \(q\) itself reduces,
after canceling its \(q\)-coefficient, to this case or is trivial.
At target \(p\), combinations of the unchanged other fibers already
lie in \(K_p\subset L\); canceling a self-coefficient again deals
with all representations.

These inclusions show that the section of the new hull at each
integer base is exactly the proposed fiber. Its projection is still
\(\operatorname{conv}(P)\), and completeness excludes any new
integer base. The hull is a full-dimensional compact convex body.
This proves both directions.

Thus \({\cal R}_p\setminus K_p\) is the exact available region for
independent monotone enlargement. In particular, if
\({\cal R}_p=K_p\), even a tiny proper enlargement is impossible
with all the other fibers fixed.

## 3. A checkable reserve facet

Let \(G\) be a facet of \(K_p\), with outward unit normal \(n_G\).
For each inequality \(u\cdot x\le B\) in (2), compute
\(B-\max_{x\in G}u\cdot x\). Suppose every such number is positive.
This is a finite check at the vertices of \(G\). Equivalently,
\[
                         G\subset\operatorname{int}{\cal R}_p.   \tag{4}
\]
When (2) has no inequalities the condition is automatic.

Replace the single own-fiber facet inequality
\[
 n_G\cdot x\le h_p(n_G)
 \quad\text{by}\quad
 n_G\cdot x\le h_p(n_G)+t,                               \tag{5}
\]
keeping the other own-fiber inequalities unchanged. Write the
resulting polytope as \(K_p(t)\).

**Lemma 2.** For all sufficiently small \(t>0\), (5) yields a
bounded positive-volume polytope satisfying
\[
 K_p\subset K_p(t)\subset{\cal R}_p.
 \]
Consequently it is an actual change of only fiber \(p\).

**Proof.** The finite normal directions have not changed, so the
recession cone is unchanged and remains \(\{0\}\). For bounded
small thresholds the polytopes are uniformly bounded and converge
in Hausdorff distance to \(K_p\). This also follows directly by
contracting about a strict interior point to absorb a small
threshold error. The new points violate only the old inequality
of \(G\); every accumulation point of such new points as \(t\to0\)
therefore lies in \(G\). The finite strictly positive gaps in (4)
give a neighborhood of the compact \(G\) contained in
\({\cal R}_p\). All the added points belong to that neighborhood
for small \(t\). Theorem 1 proves actual compatibility.

Notice that (4) is a local condition on one facet and all its
outgoing constraints. It does not require strict compatibility
elsewhere in the family.

## 4. Exact first-order response of every fixed closed cap

Put \(A=\mathcal H_{d-1}(G)>0\). Let \(\mu_t\) be the actual mixed
volume of the changed family. Then
\[
 M(t)=M+tA+o(t).                                       \tag{6}
\]
For a fixed closed ambient halfspace
\(H=\{a\cdot z+v\cdot x\ge b\}\), define its outward trace on \(G\)
by the actual one-sided limit
\[
 \chi_H^+(x)=\lim_{s\downarrow0}
        1_H(p,x+s n_G).
 \]
The limit exists everywhere. It is the ordinary cap indicator
off its boundary. On the boundary its value is 1 if
\(v\cdot n_G\ge0\), and 0 if \(v\cdot n_G<0\). In the equality
case the point stays on the closed cap boundary.
Then
\[
 \mu_t(H)=\mu_0(H)+tA_H+o(t),\qquad
 A_H=\int_G\chi_H^+\,d\mathcal H_{d-1}.                 \tag{7}
\]

For completeness, away from the edges of \(G\), the added region
is an outward prism of height \(t+o(t)\). Its other boundary
faces contribute only edge-neighborhood remainders. A compact
patch exhausts the facet, and the total added thickness is
uniformly \(O(t)\), proving (6) by Fubini and then (7).
At a transverse cap intersection the facet boundary is null.
At a coincident cap, an outward-added strip belongs to the
outside-oriented cap and not to the inside-oriented cap,
exactly as encoded by \(\chi_H^+\).
For a pure-integer cap its trace is the entire moving fiber
or empty, including the case of a whole fiber on its boundary.
For \(d=1\), facet measure is endpoint counting measure and
the same formulas follow from interval lengths.

Thus the fixed normalized cap response is exactly
\[
 \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{0+}
       \frac{\mu_t(H)}{M(t)}
   =\frac{A_H-\beta_H A}{M},\qquad
        \beta_H=\mu_0(H)/M.                            \tag{8}
\]
All oblique orientations and closed boundary cases are included
in (7)--(8).

## 5. A regular critical-circuit descent test

Here is a precise additional consequence for finite selected
critical circuits. Its regularity hypotheses are explicit;
they are not claimed for all active caps at an arbitrary
attained minimum.

Let \(Q=\beta M\) be the actual maximum raw depth. At each
deepest base choose a finite positive circuit of caps
\[
 H_{ij}=\{a_{ij}\cdot z+v_{ij}\cdot x\ge b_{ij}\},
 \quad |v_{ij}|=1,\quad \mu_0(H_{ij})=Q,
\]
with positive coefficients \(\rho_{ij}\), satisfying
\[
 \sum_j\rho_{ij}v_{ij}=0,\qquad
 \sum_j\rho_{ij}(b_{ij}-a_{ij}\cdot p_i)=0.             \tag{9}
\]
Thus the caps cover the entire continuous plane at \(p_i\).
Assume the remaining bases have fixed finite whole-plane
cap covers whose masses are strictly below \(Q\).

Assume each selected critical cap has a two-sided threshold
expansion with \(S_{ij}>0\):
\[
 \mu_0(H_{ij}(b_{ij}+s))=Q-S_{ij}s+o(|s|).
 \]
Also assume its boundary has zero \((d-1)\)-measure on \(G\).
This last condition excludes a coincidence on the moving
facet; without it moving the cap and the facet can have an
additional min/max branch and the following linear formula
must not be used.

Define
\[
 \kappa_{ij}=\frac{\rho_{ij}/S_{ij}}
                    {\sum_l\rho_{il}/S_{il}},\qquad
 \sigma_i(G)=\frac1A\sum_j\kappa_{ij}A_{H_{ij}}.          \tag{10}
\]
There are actual threshold changes preserving (9) for which
all caps of group \(i\) have common first-order mass response
\[
                         T_i=A\sigma_i(G).
 \]
Indeed take threshold velocities
\(\dot b_{ij}=(A_{H_{ij}}-T_i)/S_{ij}\).
Equation (10) gives \(\sum_j\rho_{ij}\dot b_{ij}=0\).
The cap response is \(A_{H_{ij}}-S_{ij}\dot b_{ij}=T_i\).
The same formula under simultaneous body and threshold
movement follows by the slab expansion: the threshold strip
and added facet strip have overlap \(o(t)\), since their
intersection on \(G\) is null.

The shifted groups still cover their entire assigned fiber
planes. The fixed slack covers handle every other fiber
for small \(t\); their positive budget gaps persist. Hence
\[
 \limsup_{t\downarrow0}
 \frac{D(K(t))-\beta}{t}
 \le\frac{A}{M}\max_i\bigl(\sigma_i(G)-\beta\bigr).       \tag{11}
\]
In particular, if every \(\sigma_i(G)<\beta\), the reserve
facet produces a strict actual decrease of maximum depth.
At a local minimum with these hypotheses, each reserve
facet and each selected system of critical circuits must
therefore have at least one group with
\(\sigma_i(G)\ge\beta\).

This is a checkable feasibility-and-flux test, not a theorem
that positive midpoint or centroid defect supplies a facet
satisfying it. The companion exact examples show that
positive defects need not even make either endpoint's
independent enlargement region larger than its original
body.
